Content:
So far, we've proved that a circle [MATH: \mathcal C] is similar to the unit circle [MATH: \mathcal U] in cases involving just a single similarity transformation.

Before we move on to more complex cases, we note that similarity in two-dimensional figures possesses the properties of reflexivity, symmetricity, and transitivity.

Content:
More formally, suppose that [MATH: \mathcal F_1, \mathcal F_2,] and [MATH: \mathcal F_3] are two-dimensional geometric figures. Then, the following properties hold:

Content:
- The reflexive property of similarity:
[MATH: \mathcal F_1 \sim \mathcal F_1]
This states that every figure is similar to itself.
- The symmetric property of similarity:
[MATH: \textrm{If}\: \mathcal F_1 \sim \mathcal F_2, \textrm{then}\: \mathcal F_2 \sim \mathcal F_1]
This states that if the first figure is similar to the second, the second must be similar to the first.
- The transitive property of similarity:
[MATH: \textrm{If}\: F_1 \sim \mathcal F_2 \:\textrm{and}\: F_2 \sim \mathcal F_3,\textrm{then}\: F_1 \sim \mathcal F_3]
This states that if the first figure is similar to the second, and the second is similar to the third, the first must be similar to the third.
